column5: Ox knows owner; donkey knows manger
column6: The commentary says a stray camel has an unknown owner but livestock recognize their master; Isaiah turns ox and donkey's recognition into a rebuke because Israel does not know its Lord.

column5: Birds know appointed seasons
column6: The commentary contrasts animals that know their owner with people more astray than cattle; Jeremiah says migratory birds know their times while God's people do not know his ordinance.

column5: Donkey sees the angel and leaves the road
column6: The commentary makes guidance a question of following a lead animal; here Balaam's donkey detects the blocked path that the human seer misses, reversing human and animal discernment.

column5: Straying ox or sheep must be returned
column6: The commentary's dālle camel has escaped its owner; Torah treats a neighbor's stray livestock as recoverable property and forbids ignoring it.

column5: Keep the animal until its absent owner seeks it
column6: The commentary defines the stray camel as remaining where its owner is unknown; this law makes the finder temporarily responsible when the owner is not nearby.

column5: Return an enemy's straying ox or donkey
column6: The commentary's ownerless camel prompts the question of the finder's relation to its owner; Exodus extends recovery duty even to an enemy's animal.

column5: The Lord as shepherd; the speaker as sheep
column6: The commentary links Rabb to an animal's owner; the psalm names God as shepherd and makes the human speaker part of his flock.

column5: Shepherd settles sheep in green pasture
column6: The commentary develops a herd remaining at its pasture and land pleasing for grazing; this verse joins the shepherd's care to settled, nourishing pasture.

column5: God leads on right paths
column6: The commentary turns ihdinā into a flock's following its foreleader; the shepherd leads the speaker on right paths, joining guidance to the animal image.

column5: Forest beasts and cattle belong to God
column6: The commentary glosses its source form rabb (رَبّ) as owner and begins with an owned camel herd; this verse explicitly places wild beasts and cattle under divine ownership.

column5: The world and all in it belong to God
column6: The commentary's source gloss says the Rabb of each thing is its owner; the psalm applies ownership universally, beyond a single herd.

column5: Wanderers lost in an empty desert without a town
column6: The commentary describes a camel escaping and remaining in a desolate place; this psalm opens with people wandering in waste without an inhabited settlement.

column5: The lost cry to the Lord for help
column6: The commentary pairs an ownerless animal's lost state with the surah's request for help; here the wilderness wanderers cry out and receive divine rescue.

column5: God leads them by a straight way
column6: The commentary makes the camel's foreleader an image for asking to be guided on the straight path; this verse explicitly joins divine leading to a straight way.

column5: God leads his people like a flock through the wilderness
column6: The commentary's flock follows its leading animal; the psalm depicts God leading his people as sheep through a wilderness journey.

column5: People are God's pasture flock and hear his voice
column6: The commentary joins herd ownership to following a leader; the psalm calls the people sheep of God's hand and immediately calls them to hear his voice.

column5: A lost sheep asks its owner to seek it
column6: The commentary's dālle camel is lost from its owner; the psalmist calls himself a lost sheep and asks God to seek his servant.

column5: Israel must not be left like sheep without a shepherd
column6: The commentary says the request for guidance entails a foreleader whom the rest follow; Moses asks for a successor so the congregation will not be leaderless like sheep.

column5: Lost sheep are led astray by their shepherds
column6: The commentary contrasts a herd's leader with the danger of losing the way; Jeremiah's people are lost sheep whose own shepherds mislead them, making the guide itself culpable.

column5: Scattered sheep have no shepherd to seek them
column6: The commentary's stray camel remains in a wasteland with no known owner; Ezekiel pictures scattered sheep with no shepherd and no one searching for them.

column5: God himself searches for his sheep
column6: The commentary's lost camel has an unknown owner; Ezekiel answers with God personally seeking and rescuing his scattered flock.

column5: A shepherd gathers a scattered flock
column6: The commentary's animal is lost in a desolate place; this verse compares God's search to a shepherd inspecting his flock and rescuing sheep dispersed on a cloudy day.

column5: Israel is God's pasture flock
column6: The commentary links an animal's owner with its herd; Ezekiel closes by identifying Israel as God's human flock and God as their God.

column5: The wild donkey is released from its bonds
column6: The commentary distinguishes an owned, tamed camel from ownerless wild herds; Job asks who freed the wild donkey, marking its opposite relation to human ownership.

column5: The wilderness is the wild donkey's home
column6: The commentary's camel is stranded in a desolate place while wild asses live outside owned herds; Job makes the wilderness the wild donkey's dwelling.

column5: The wild donkey searches the mountains for pasture
column6: The commentary develops pasture as the place a herd stays and names wild-ass herds; Job gives the untamed animal a mountain range to roam for grazing.

column5: The wild ox will not serve a human master
column6: The commentary's dictionary form al-baʿīr al-muʿabbad is a tarred/tamed camel; Job sets against it a wild ox that will not submit to service.

column5: The wild ox cannot be harnessed to plow
column6: The commentary describes a subdued camel within an owned herd; Job specifies the practical limit of human control over the wild ox.

column5: God teaches and points out the way
column6: The commentary makes ihdinā a request for the leader of a following herd; the psalm has God promise to instruct and guide the person in the way.

column5: Horse and mule need bit and bridle to be guided
column6: The commentary treats the flock's voluntarily followed foreleader as an image for guidance; the psalm contrasts an instructed person with animals that must be restrained to come near.

column5: The king goes out before the people
column6: The commentary cites the dictionary form milk (مَلِك) for the animal at the head of a herd; Hebrew melek is its Semitic cognate, and Israel asks for a king who will go before them in battle.

column5: David is taken from ewes to shepherd Israel
column6: The commentary's malik is the animal ahead of a herd; this verse makes a former shepherd the ruler appointed over God's people.

column5: David shepherds and guides with integrity
column6: The commentary joins a lead animal to guidance of those following; this verse presents Israel's ruler as one who shepherds and guides the people.

column5: Pleasant boundary lines and a good inheritance
column6: The commentary labels root ن ع م and says camels are called en-naʿam for the good and blessing they bring; Hebrew nʿm in this verse describes pleasant boundaries beside a good inheritance, a cognate semantic field rather than an animal term.

column5: Blessing includes cattle and flock offspring
column6: The commentary explains its source form en-naʿam as livestock that brings good and blessing; Deuteronomy lists the increase of cattle and flock among God's covenant blessings.

column5: A faithful ruler shepherds the Lord's flock in pasture
column6: The commentary's malik is the herd's foreleader and its hadī guides followers; this Jewish royal hope joins a shepherd-ruler to faithful care and a pasture where sheep do not stumble.

column5: God turns people back like a shepherd his flock
column6: The commentary's camel is lost from its owner; Sirach compares God's correction and teaching to a shepherd bringing back his flock.

column5: All things are God's own
column6: The commentary's source gloss calls the Rabb of everything its owner; Wisdom grounds God's sparing care in the claim that all things belong to him.

column5: A shepherd searches for one sheep that strayed
column6: The commentary defines a dālle camel as escaped and ownerless; Jesus' parable gives the lost animal an owner who searches until he finds it.

column5: The found sheep is brought back and celebrated
column6: The commentary leaves the lost camel separated from its owner; Luke's shepherd returns with the found sheep and gathers friends to celebrate, supplying a recovery scene.

column5: Heaven rejoices over a sinner who repents
column6: The commentary compares human misguidance with a camel that is lost from its owner; Luke interprets the recovered sheep as the sinner who turns back, connecting return to repentance.

column5: A shepherd seeks a wandering sheep
column6: The commentary's lost camel has no known owner; Matthew's parable has a shepherd leave the ninety-nine to seek the one that wandered.

column5: The shepherd rejoices when the sheep is found
column6: The commentary describes the camel only while lost; Matthew emphasizes the owner's joy at recovery.

column5: The Father wills that none of the little ones perish
column6: The commentary contrasts a lost animal with humans more lost than cattle; Matthew uses the shepherd image to say the Father seeks the vulnerable rather than letting one perish.

column5: People are harassed like sheep without a shepherd
column6: The commentary says the request for guidance needs a leader ahead of the flock; Jesus sees the crowds as sheep without a shepherd, making the human need for guidance explicit.

column5: A shepherdless crowd receives teaching
column6: The commentary makes a leading animal the image behind the request to be guided; Jesus sees the crowd as sheep without a shepherd and begins teaching them, acting as guide.

column5: The shepherd calls his own sheep by name
column6: The commentary says a brand identifies whose camel it is and that the stray camel's owner is unknown; John's shepherd knows and summons each animal as his own.

column5: The shepherd goes ahead and the sheep follow
column6: The commentary's malik is the animal at the head of the herd and its hadī leads the others; Jesus describes the shepherd walking ahead and his sheep following.

column5: Sheep do not follow a stranger
column6: The commentary says the herd follows its foreleader; John adds recognition as the criterion, since sheep flee from an unfamiliar voice.

column5: The shepherd knows his sheep and they follow him
column6: The commentary joins owner, animal, and following leader; Jesus says he knows his sheep and they follow his voice.

column5: Mary addresses Jesus as ῥαββουνί
column6: The commentary's dictionary form rabb (رَبّ) is glossed 'owner'; John's Greek preserves the Aramaic rbb title 'my teacher,' a related Semitic master-title used for a teacher rather than a livestock owner.

column5: Straying sheep return to the shepherd and overseer
column6: The commentary calls the camel dālle when lost from its owner; Peter says his readers were straying like sheep but have returned to the shepherd who watches them.

column5: The Lamb shepherds people to springs of water
column6: The commentary combines a leading animal with pasture and the request for guidance; Revelation's Lamb becomes shepherd and guides people to springs.

column5: Followers go wherever the Lamb goes
column6: The commentary says a herd follows the lead animal and makes this the force of asking for guidance; Revelation describes people following the Lamb wherever he goes.

column5: Spotted and speckled animals distinguish Jacob's flock
column6: The commentary says a brand shows whose camel it is; Jacob proposes coat patterns as a visible way to distinguish which animals are his, though these are natural markings, not brands.

column5: A mark distinguishes those spared from judgment
column6: The commentary's camel brand identifies the animal's owner; Ezekiel's mark distinguishes people to be spared, shifting identification from property to protection.

column5: The wise are put to shame and reject the Lord's word
column6: The commentary contrasts animals that recognize an owner with people more astray than cattle; Jeremiah's immediate context extends the bird comparison to the people's rejection of divine instruction.

column5: People are God's flock and pasture sheep
column6: The commentary connects an animal to its owner; this liturgical line identifies worshippers as God's people and sheep, adding communal belonging to the flock image.

column5: Earth and its fullness belong to the Lord
column6: The commentary glosses rabb as the owner of each thing; the psalm states the same universal ownership in a creation hymn.

column5: Hebrew ʿābad means to work or serve
column6: The commentary labels root ع ب د in naʿbudu and quotes al-baʿīr al-muʿabbad, a tamed/tarred camel; Genesis uses the cognate Hebrew root for the human's work in Eden, preserving a service/work sense without making the garden animal imagery.

column5: Hebrew nʿm means pleasant
column6: The commentary labels source root ن ع م and explains en-naʿam through good and blessing; Hebrew nʿm describes pleasantness here, a cognate sense-family rather than a reference to livestock.

column5: A bit directs a horse's whole body
column6: The commentary says the horse's hādī may be its neck or the foremost group; James supplies a different concrete steering image, the bit by which a human turns a horse.

column5: God's servants receive a seal on their foreheads
column6: The commentary's brand identifies the camel's owner; Revelation's seal marks those who belong to God and are protected, transferring ownership-identification to people.

column5: The beast's mark identifies its adherents
column6: The commentary's camel brand indicates whose herd an animal belongs to; Revelation's imposed mark signals allegiance to the beast, a hostile counterpart rather than the same kind of ownership.

column5: A shepherd searches for his one lost sheep
column6: The commentary's dālle camel escapes and remains away from its owner; Thomas preserves a lost-sheep parable in which the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine and seeks the stray.

column5: Hebrew melek is a ruler who goes before the people
column6: The commentary's dictionary form milk (مَلِك) names the animal at the head of a herd; Hebrew melek is a cognate ruler-title, and this verse gives the king the specific role of going before Israel.
